item.title: SIR applies a decade of exclusion lessons perfected on welfare schemes
item.description: Concerns about opaque software, technological interventions and excessive centralisation that affected India’s poorest now extend to the right to vote.
item.content:encoded:
The Special Intensive Revision of India’s voter rolls has sparked concerns about the widespread disenfranchisement of eligible voters and that it is becoming a citizenship test. Its method is not new, but what is different this time is that it threatens the right to vote.

Digital tools have served the rolls since the 1990s: voter identity cards from 1993, computerised rolls, voting machines in every constituency by the 2004 general election and photo rolls nationwide by 2009. Through those years, rolls were corrected one application at a time, with officers deciding each case – former Chief Election Commissioner SY Quraishi says they were already about 99% accurate. From 2015 the Commission set out to “purify” the rolls by matching them against Aadhaar records.

The SIR, which began in Bihar in June 2025, completes the turn. It denies the roll on which the 2024 general election was held any presumption of eligibility, and presumes eligible only those found on a roll two decades old, so that everyone under about 40 can be linked only through a parent or grandparent or by producing supporting documents.

item.title: Spain: 64 dead as two high-speed trains collide
item.description: The crash – Spain’s second major railway accident this year – followed a January collision on the same line that killed 46 persons.
item.content:encoded:
Sixty-four persons died after two high-speed trains collided in central Spain on Wednesday, reported AFP. Regional authorities said that the toll was expected to rise.

At least 80 persons had been injured due to the collision, including 50 who were in serious condition, BBC reported.

The collision occurred in the province of Toledo, south of Madrid, when a train operated by state-owned rail company Renfe struck the rear of a stationary train run by private operator Iryo.

The Iryo train had stopped near Toledo because of a signal fault, reported Reuters. The Renfe train struck it at high speed, causing several carriages on both trains to derail.

Renfe said its train had been authorised to continue its journey before the collision with the train that remained stationary “for reasons we do not know”.

The crash is Spain’s second major railway accident this year. In January, 46 persons were killed when two trains operated by Renfe and Iryo collided on the same line, Reuters reported.

item.title: Virginia Woolf’s ‘Orlando’, the ultimate shapeshifter, is now a madcap graphic novel
item.description: A speculative romp across time and the gender binary, ‘Orlando’ was inspired by Woolf’s love affair with the aristocrat Vita Sackville-West.
item.content:encoded:
“Orlando had become a woman – there is no denying it. But in every other respect, Orlando remained precisely as he had been.”

“Orlando was a man until the age of thirty; when he became a woman and has remained so ever since.”

With their unabashed acceptance of gender fluidity, these declarations ring with the politics of our present moment. They would be at home in a contemporary trans memoir or Instagram caption. Over on X, they would send a certain children’s author and her followers into a predictable frenzy.

Remarkably, however, these sentences were penned almost a century ago. In 1928, to be precise, when Virginia Woolf published Orlando: A Biography, the story of a 16th-century English nobleman who lives for four centuries and one day wakes up in the body of a woman.

A speculative romp across time and the gender binary, Orlando was inspired by Woolf’s love affair with the aristocrat Vita Sackville-West, a fellow member of the very queer milieu of modernist writers and artists known as the Bloomsbury Group.

Long beloved as a trailblazing queer text, described by Sackville-West’s son as “the longest and most charming love letter in literature”, Orlando has now been given fresh life as a graphic novel authored by German writer and illustrator Susanne Kuhlendahl.

item.title: Bihar seeks resolution as India’s Ganga water sharing treaty with Bangladesh expires this year
item.description: Some experts do not accept claims that the treaty is affecting the state while others say its needs must be factored before renewing the agreement.
item.content:encoded:
As the Ganga water-sharing treaty between India and Bangladesh ends this year, Bihar seeks to resolve its long-standing demands before the treaty is renewed.

The treaty, signed in December 1996, governs the sharing of the Ganga river’s water between upstream India and downstream Bangladesh, particularly during the lean season when river flows are low.

Under the treaty, during the lean period from January to June, if water at the Farakka barrage is less than 70,000 cubic feet per second (cusecs), India and Bangladesh each get half. If the water at the barrage is between 70,000 and 75,000 cusecs, Bangladesh will be assured 35,000 cusecs, and the rest will go to India. If the water is 75,000 cusecs or more, India will get an assured 40,000 cusecs, and Bangladesh will get the rest.

The agreement further says Bangladesh will get a guaranteed flow of 35,000 cusecs on the first and last ten days of April and 27,633 cusecs between April 11 and 20. If the Ganga’s flow falls below 50,000 cusecs in any ten-day period, the two governments will enter immediate consultations to make emergency adjustments.

For decades, Bihar’s political leaders have argued that the Ganga water-sharing treaty with Bangladesh does not adequately account for the state’s water needs.

item.title: Mythological fiction: After Kurukshetra, Shakuni is a man forged in the fires of familial massacre
item.description: An excerpt from ‘The Hawk’s Quest’, by Deepa Agarwal.
item.content:encoded:
A shapeless half-moon hung in the inky sky, spreading pallid light, when Shakuni reached his young wife’s chambers. He had not been able to meet Arshi the whole day. The news must have travelled to her and he yearned to share his concern with her, to find the much-needed ballast in her calm steady gaze.

“It’s been a long day for you,” she murmured as he entered, rising from her couch in a fluid, graceful movement. The room was sparsely furnished – a few rugs on the stone floor, two couches spread with woollen shawls, oil lamps placed in alcoves indenting the grey unadorned walls, painted mud water pots on wooden stands. The odour of burning oil filled the air along with the fragrance of the rose water she loved to use.

“Have you eaten?” she asked. The flickering light of the lamp outlined the sharp curve of her cheekbones, offsetting the pert nose and wide mouth.

He realised that he was ravenous. In the tumult of the day, he had only managed to sip a few mouthfuls of water and buttermilk.

item.title: Hardeep Singh Puri named BJP candidate for Madhya Pradesh Rajya Sabha bye-poll
item.description: The Union minister, whose current term ends on November 25, needs to be re-elected to either House of Parliament within six months to remain in the Cabinet.
item.content:encoded:
The Bharatiya Janata Party on Wednesday named Union minister Hardeep Singh Puri as its candidate for the Rajya Sabha bye-election in Madhya Pradesh.

The bye-poll, scheduled for November 12, became necessary after L Murugan resigned from the Upper House of Parliament and as the Union minister on October 14. His Rajya Sabha term was to end in April 2030.

Based on the composition of the Madhya Pradesh Assembly, Puri is expected to win the seat unopposed.

Puri became a Rajya Sabha member from Uttar Pradesh in January 2018, four months after becoming a Union minister. His current term will end on November 25.

He was not among the BJP candidates announced for the Rajya Sabha polls in Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand and West Bengal earlier this month. Puri is not a member of the Lok Sabha.

A minister who is not a member of either House of Parliament for six consecutive months ceases to be a part of the Cabinet.

Puri’s candidature comes amid questions since early this year after his name came up in the “Epstein files”.

item.title: Para-athlete Neeraj Yadav dies allegedly by suicide
item.description: Yadav had missed the Asian Para Games in Japan earlier this month because of a doping suspension.
item.content:encoded:
Para-athlete Neeraj Yadav, who had won three Asian Para Games gold medals before being suspended for a doping violation, died allegedly by suicide at his home in Delhi on Tuesday, PTI reported. He was 42.

Yadav, who was from Uttar Pradesh, had missed the Asian Para Games in Japan from October 18 to October 24 because of the doping suspension.

The National Anti-Doping Agency provisionally suspended him in October 2023 after he tested positive for stanozolol, an anabolic steroid. The medication increases strength and can give athletes unfair advantage in sporting events.

He competed in the F55 category, which includes seated field events such as shot put, discus and javelin. Yadav played wheelchair tennis from 2005 to 2012 before moving to para-athletics. He was diagnosed with post-polio residual paralysis at the age of seven.

S Satyanarayana, head coach of the Indian para-athletics team, said Yadav would have been looking forward to competing at the games. “Medals at the Asian Para Games can bring substantial government cash awards and opportunities for stable employment,” the Times of India quoted him as saying.

item.title: Are probiotics necessary? Food expert Krish Ashok asks this question in his new book
item.description: An excerpt from ‘Masala Body: An Engineer’s Guide to Eating’.
item.content:encoded:
The global probiotics market is now a multi-billion-dollar industry. A supplement may contain one or several named strains, measured in colony-forming units (CFU) – a laboratory estimate of how many organisms remain capable of growing. Your colon already houses tens of trillions of microbes from hundreds of species, which makes a capsule a rounding error.

A rounding error is not the same as nothing – microbes can influence an ecosystem without becoming its majority. But the marketing claim with the enormous-looking number tells you almost nothing unless that exact strain has been shown to solve a specific problem you have.

A small but striking 2018 Weizmann Institute study tested this directly. Researchers sampled the intestinal wall rather than relying only on stool and found that a standard probiotic mixture behaved very differently between people. In some, the newcomers briefly settled; in others, they passed through like the visitor in Satyajit Ray’s Agantuk.

After antibiotics, that particular probiotic mixture actually delayed the return of the original microbial community compared with leaving it alone, a bit like what happens when politically connected squatters occupy your land. Congress leader Rahul Gandhi on Wednesday alleged that the Union government was “criminally destroying” the Tata Group, the largest Indian conglomerate.

Gandhi said that no business leader had “dared to say a word” and asked how long they would “stay silent”.

Indian business is not Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Union Home Minister Amit Shah’s “plaything”, the Opposition leader said on social media.

He added that business leaders were “lacking courage” and that the Congress “will ensure justice for these crimes”.

It was not immediately clear what Gandhi was referring to. But the comments came amid a dispute within the leadership of Tata Sons, which is the holding entity of the conglomerate’s companies.

The corporate dispute mainly revolves around the reappointment of N Chandrasekaran as the executive chairman of Tata Sons and the proposed listing of the holding company on the stock market.

The New India Foundation has announced the shortlist for the 2026 Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay NIF Book Prize.

The winner will be announced in December, and the prize will be presented on December 12 at the Bangalore Literature Festival. The winning author will receive a cash prize of Rs 15 lakh.

The shortlist comprises five works of non-fiction on modern and contemporary India, all published in 2025. These five books span the making of India’s Constitution, the arc of its development since independence, and the partitions that shaped modern Asia. They also follow the lives that moved through these histories, from a statesman and diplomat to a Hindustani musician, showing how a nation is built and sustained.

The shortlist was selected by a Jury comprising Chairman of Tata Sons and Tata Group N Chandrasekaran, political scientist Niraja Gopal Jayal, partner at Trilegal Rahul Matthan, historian of science Jahnavi Phalkey, historian Srinath Raghavan, former Foreign Secretary of India Nirupama Rao, and entrepreneur Manish Sabharwal.

item.title: Cyclone Arnab: Three killed in Andhra Pradesh
item.description: Flights were affected and at least 64 trains were cancelled as the cyclonic storm completed landfall on Wednesday.
item.content:encoded:
Three persons were killed and 31 houses damaged in Andhra Pradesh as Cyclone Arnab made landfall on Wednesday, PTI quoted a National Disaster Response Force officer as saying.

The very severe cyclonic storm weakened into a severe cyclone after completing its landfall, the India Meteorological Department said.

Heavy to very heavy rain was reported in several parts of coastal Andhra Pradesh, with some areas recording more than 200 mm of rainfall, the Hindustan Times reported.

The landfall continued for six hours as the cyclone crossed the coasts of Andhra Pradesh and Yanam in Puducherry between 2 am and 8 am, with maximum sustained wind speeds of 125 km per hour to 135 km per hour.

The storm was likely to move north-northwestwards in the next 48 hours and weaken further gradually, the department said.

Samiul Sheikh, the main accused in the murder of BJP worker Sujit Mondal, was shot dead in Murshidabad district while allegedly trying to escape custody, the police said.

Sheikh and two other persons were arrested after Mondal went missing on August 28, the Hindustan Times reported. The police later recovered parts of Mondal’s body from a canal.

On Tuesday, a team of the Criminal Investigation Department took Sheikh to the Old Dak Bungalow area in Samserganj to reconstruct the crime, a police officer told PTI.

The officer said that Sheikh tried to escape while returning from the spot, snatched a firearm from a police officer and opened fire at the team.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu-led alliance was ahead of the Opposition bloc in the country’s general elections as the votes were being counted on Wednesday.

As of 4 pm Indian time, the Netanyahu-led coalition was leading in 54 of the 120 seats in Parliament, Haaretz reported. A party or an alliance needs 61 seats to form the government.

The Opposition bloc was ahead in 49 seats. The Arab parties, which are supported largely by Israel’s Palestinian minority, were leading in 17 seats.

More than 77% of the votes had been counted.

The results were largely in line with the exit polls, which showed a neck-and-neck contest between the alliances led by Netanyahu and his main rival Gadi Eisenkot, with neither predicted to secure a clear path to a governing majority.

The polling was held on Tuesday. The official results are expected by Friday.

item.title: Harsh Mander: The unlikely redemption of the 13-year-old jailed for the murder of Graham Staines
item.description: After nearly a decade in jail, Chenchu Hansda was tormented by voices in his head. This is his story.
item.content:encoded:
Graham Stuart Staines, a Christian missionary from Australia, dedicated nearly 35 years of his life healing patients of leprosy in the forest interiors of Mayurbhanj district in Odisha. In that impoverished remote forest land, there were none more despised and dispossessed than those living with leprosy. Their only hope was Global Health Dermatology care, and the compassion and friendship of Graham and his wife Gladys.

One horrific cold winter night, on January 22, 1999, Staines and his two sons were burned alive by a mob of Hindutva workers. They set fire to the station wagon in which they were sleeping. Staines and his two sons, 10-year-old Philip and six-year-old Timothy all perished in the fire.

The youngest member of the mob that set the Christian missionary and his sons on fire was 13-year-old Chenchu Hansda. This is his story, of his conviction, his long and lonely years of incarceration, his torments and ultimately his unlikely conversion as an adult man to the Christian faith.

item.title: How the mismatch between climate change and touristic aspirations is harming the Himalayas
item.description: An excerpt from Sonali Gupta’s essay in ‘The Living Himalaya: Rock, Sky, Spirit’, edited by Namita Gokhale and Malashri Lal.
item.content:encoded:
Long before Instagram discovered the “mountain aesthetic”, writers and painters had turned the Himalaya and its connected ranges into screens for every possible longing. James Hilton’s Lost Horizon condensed central and eastern Himalayan motifs into Shangri-La, a timeless sanctuary of moderation and wisdom somewhere beyond the ordinary world.

Nicholas Roerich marched through Kashmir, Ladakh and Central Asia in the 1920s, chasing legends of Shambhala and painting a long series of canvases full of cobalt ridges, luminous snows and monasteries perched like punctuation marks on cliffs. Admirers sometimes say he left hidden clues in these canvases; one suspects the mountains, if asked, would shrug and point out that the most obvious clue is the geology in the background, which everyone compliments and almost no one reads.

Eventually Roerich settled in Naggar in Kullu Valley, building a house that looks modest until you glimpse the views from its verandah. From there he continued to paint the ranges that had once been rumoured as a hidden kingdom, now treated as both subject and neighbour. Between his canvases, his role in early cultural-protection treaties, and the ongoing activity at the Urusvati Himalayan Research Institute, Roerich helped crystallise a vocabulary of Himalayan sacredness that still colours everything...

item.title: Mehran Hodiwala’s songs find the funny side of life’s uncomfortable moments
item.description: The 18-year-old Mumbai college student cannot be bothered with capitalisation in his song titles. But the feelings they deal with are anything but small.
item.content:encoded:
Three weeks ago, Mehran Hodiwala’s music suddenly hit a high note. Though the Mumbai singer-songwriter had been posting tunes on social media since 2024, he had been reaching a relatively small group of listeners. But 20 days after sharing learning, it had racked up over 10 lakh views.

For most musicians, this kind of sudden attention would be a dream come true. Hodiwala, though, is a little hesitant about what it means to have so many new listeners.

“The more ears you have listening, the more on guard you tend to get,” Hodiwala said. And being on guard, he thinks, is hardly ideal for making art.

At one point, the second-year college student worried that the burst of attention would make it impossible for him to write music. But then, he managed to compose another song, which put him somewhat at ease.

The comments under the video of learning – which is about the frustration of struggling to learn and change despite knowing better – capture some of what makes his music so appealing. “It might be the best song of all time... considering he cannot play the guitar or sing,” reads one of the top comments. “I still love it.”

item.title: Why more people are resorting to ‘DIY’ health advice and it is dangerous
item.description: Online searches may occasionally point people in the right direction, but they can also encourage unnecessary anxiety or false reassurance.
item.content:encoded:
Need treatment fast? Many people now turn to Google before a healthcare professional. From checking symptoms online to buying medicines online and taking advice from social media influencers, healthcare is increasingly becoming a do-it-yourself activity.

Convenience is a big part of the appeal. Information is available instantly – no need to wait weeks to see a GP – and online communities often provide reassurance from people with similar experiences.

Researching a health problem on the internet can feel empowering. But while greater access to health information has benefits, the rise of DIY healthcare also comes with risks. Research suggests that diagnosing and treating yourself, or relying on unqualified sources for advice, can lead to mistakes, the wrong use of medicines and delays in getting professional help.

The internet has changed the way people access health information. A few decades ago, someone worried about a symptom might consult a doctor, pharmacist or medical reference book. Today, a search engine can generate thousands of results in seconds.

The problem is that not all health information online is reliable. Websites can be difficult to navigate, use complex language, or provide incomplete, outdated, or inaccurate information.

item.title: Rage, lust and radical growth: Five must-read menopause novels
item.description: Terms like ‘meno-lit’ and ‘hot flush noir’ are surfacing – just as ‘chick-lit’ was once used to patronise commercial women’s fiction.
item.content:encoded:
Novels featuring older female characters enduring the joint horrors of ageism and misogyny have been around for a while. But fiction foregrounding the specifics of midlife hormonal changes is a surprisingly recent phenomenon.

Given the medical profiles of menopause (and its predecessor, perimenopause), perhaps it’s unsurprising that wellness guides and health-related memoirs have led the way.

Journalist Sam Baker’s pioneering The Shift, actor Naomi Watts’ Dare I Say It and Darcey Steinke’s Flash Count Diary combine personal experience with research. Handbooks like Liz Earle’s The Good Menopause Guide and Dr Mary Claire Havers’ series on perimenopause and menopause focus on disseminating facts.

Now that fiction is catching up, terms like “meno-lit” and “hot flush noir” are surfacing – just as “chick-lit” was once used to patronise commercial women’s fiction. Hopefully, the increasing visibility of menopausal protagonists will move past the novelty phase and become a mainstay of the novel. After all, the stages of menopause are a universal female experience. Surely, it’s time they were integrated into the wider realms of fiction.

Here are five novels tackling the early stages of menopause with fervour.

item.title: The seven crumbling pillars of India’s democracy
item.description: It is becoming painfully evident that the ailment affecting Indian democracy is not one that a change in government can cure.
item.content:encoded:
A century has passed since the publication of the autobiography of TE Lawrence, popularly known as Lawrence of Arabia. The title Seven Pillars of Wisdom is drawn from the Book of Proverbs in the Bible: “Wisdom hath builded her house, she hath hewn out her seven pillars.”

How appropriate, then, that in their wisdom, the founders of our Constitution went in for democracy as the form of government that would guide independent India’s destiny.

As it transpires, the structure of democracy in India rests on seven pillars, namely (i) legislature (ii) executive (political and bureaucratic) (iii) political parties (iv) judiciary (v) independent institutions (vi) media and (vii) civil society.

As of today, all the pillars appear shaky, threatening the future of democracy, although it could be argued that structural weaknesses in the Indian democratic edifice have existed right from 1947.

Let us start with the legislatures, both at the union and state levels. Cracks appeared in the post-Nehruvian era. The 2025 Digital Personal Data Protection Rules were notified by the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology in November 2025, bringing into effect the 2023 Digital Personal Data Protection Act.

Section 44(3) of the Act imposes a blanket ban on the disclosure of personal information without defining what constitutes “personal information”.

My mother suffered from bipolar disorder. We didn’t have a name for the illness but we experienced its effects in bizarre ways. One late evening, as I sat doing my homework, my mother came into the room, agitated and manic. She ordered me to get up and follow her to the terrace. She said that I had no redeeming qualities, nothing going for me, nothing to live for. It would be best if I jumped off the roof with her.

I should not be afraid, she said, because we would hold hands. When I tried to run away, she threw me on the ground and pummelled my chest with her bare feet. My brother and sister heard my yelling and rescued me.

item.title: Lula’s ‘miracle’ victory buys time for Brazil, resonates globally amid rise of far-right
item.description: The world’s fourth-largest democracy has now bucked the trend of far-right gains, and is a symbol that democrats elsewhere will not ignore.
item.content:encoded:
Three weeks ago, Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s political obituaries had all been written.

The far-right presidential candidate, Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the jailed former President Jair Bolsonaro, had come out of the first round of the presidential election with a lead that looked impossible to overcome.

At 80 years old, Lula seemed headed for a quiet exit after four decades at the centre of Brazilian political life.

On Sunday, however, Lula proved everyone wrong. He won the runoff and secured a fourth non-consecutive term as Brazil’s president.

A night of firsts

The election result is unprecedented in Brazilian politics in at least three ways.

First, no Brazilian presidential candidate had ever won the first round and then lost the runoff. Since the two-round system was adopted by the 1988 Brazilian Constitution, the first-round leader had always gone on to win.

Lula broke that pattern by turning a defeat of around 2.2 million votes in the first round into a solid victory, in three weeks.

Second, no Brazilian president has ever been elected to four terms. When his new term ends, Lula will have governed Brazil for 16 (non-consecutive) years – the longest democratically elected tenure in the country’s history.

is an art.
is warfare.
is a way of living.
is in my blood.
is all I have ever known.
is Kannappa Chekavar.

Kannappa Chekavar

is my acha,
my father.

He is disciplined and strict.
He is loving and encouraging too.

He is also the greatest
Kalari master of Kadathanadu.

He is unmatchable,
unbeatable
in this art of war
fought with every weapon used in close combat.
Wooden staffs, swords, daggers, maces
are mere toys in his hands.

It is said he knows more adavukkal – combat moves –
than anyone else practising Kalaripayattu.
It is also said
that he has never taught
all nineteen of them to anyone.

He has shared all
but the last technique,
the most cunning one,
keeping it close to his heart,
waiting for that special student
worthy enough to earn this secret.

No pity

The consequence of being ten minutes late
is an extra hour of practice.

Breathless and exhausted,
I gaze longingly
at the other students leaving the class.
They must be off to the vacant field
by the village pond
to hang out and play
before the sun sets for the day.

Control your breathing, Unniarcha!

item.title: Seven foreigners in terror-related probe get bail yet Indian undertrials struggle to access rights
item.description: The broader concern is the protections in law are unevenly accessible.
item.content:encoded:
A Delhi Special Court’s decision to allow seven foreign nationals under National Investigation Agency investigation in a terrorism-related case to travel home for a month raises a constitutional question: how should criminal law balance national security, investigative deadlines and personal liberty?

The accused, an American national, Matthew Aaron VanDyke and six Ukrainian citizens were arrested in March 2026. The allegations included drone assembly, electronic warfare training and support to ethnic armed organisations along the Indo-Myanmar border.

However, after the statutory period for filing a chargesheet expired, the NIA’s report omitted substantive charges under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967, and instead cited regulatory violations under the Foreigners Act, 1946. The agency maintained that its wider investigation into scheduled terrorism offences continued.

The Special Court for the NIA at Rouse Avenue, New Delhi, granted default bail and later allowed the accused to travel abroad, subject to personal bonds and diplomatic undertakings. They did not decide the merits of the allegations or represent judicial leniency; they enforced a statutory deadline. The central question is not why these foreign nationals secured release, but why comparable safeguards remain difficult for many Indian undertrials to exercise.

item.title: In a new book, Gopalkrishna Gandhi studies his grandfather Mahatma Gandhi’s views on Hinduism
item.description: ‘Whenever there is distress which one cannot remove, one must fast and pray.’
item.content:encoded:
“My religion teaches me that whenever there is distress which one cannot remove, one must fast and pray.”

India has had a tradition of fasting as a means of self-denial, self-purification, and self-mortification. This is an integral part of India’s religious and cultural history. Fasting on certain given days of the month and week, and on certain days connected with epic lore, such as on Mahashivaratri, makes fasts more than integral to Hinduism; it makes them vital and essential to it. In the Jaina tradition, fasting is even higher in the order of observances, as in Gandhi’s description of his Jain-influenced mother fasting unfailingly and cheerfully, having been seen earlier in this narrative. And Indian Muslims, of course, observe the annual fasts in the month of Ramzan punctiliously, Gandhi noting the practice with admiration in his illustrious colleague, Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan.

item.title: A new Brahmin-first party in UP symbolises a growing disquiet among BJP’s core voters
item.description: Some voters say they will pick the party best placed to defeat the BJP.

Since February this year, an office space in Lucknow’s Sapru Marg has become the home of an audacious political experiment. Every day, a handful of men gather here and brainstorm how they can subvert the Bharatiya Janata Party in the upcoming assembly elections in Uttar Pradesh.

Curiously, the men admit to having been BJP voters all their lives. They are mostly Brahmins, the privileged caste group that is a core constituency of the Hindutva party.

“The BJP was our party,” says Rajesh Shukla, a businessman who is a regular visitor here. “It has now been hijacked by backwards.”

The businessman was referring to other backward classes, or OBCs, a collection of castes that make up nearly half of UP’s population. Traditionally, the BJP has been seen as a party catering to upper-caste Hindus. Its earliest political architects like Deendayal Upadhyaya, Atal Bihari Vajpayee and Murli Manohar Joshi were Brahmins from UP.

However, over the past decade, it has won two consecutive state elections after successfully wooing OBC and Scheduled Caste voters.

This strategy might now come with a cost. The upper castes, especially Brahmins, feel that they have lost ownership of a party they considered their own. “Brahmins were the pillars in the house of BJP,” said Rajendra Nath Tripathi, the leader...

item.title: Why rats are on the ballot in Canada’s civic elections
item.description: Rodents point to broader societal concerns about housing, public services and civic engagement.
item.content:encoded:
Rats are on the ballot in Canadian municipal elections this fall, with several political parties promising to tackle city rat problems. While rats may seem like a niche election issue, they can point to broader societal concerns about housing, public services and civic engagement.

Rats are ubiquitous urban residents that cities have attempted to evict for centuries. Often portrayed as dirty pests and bringers of plague, they can harbour pathogens that cause illnesses to people and pets, like rat bite fever and leptospirosis.

So why have cities had so little success in reducing rat numbers?

Well, rats are synanthropes, species that benefit from living alongside humans, and have adapted remarkably well to our paved, cacophonic and bustling streets. Cities provide abundant resources for rats to thrive: food scraps are meals; standing water on sidewalks supplies drinking water; and cracks in buildings offer access to shelter.

Municipal policies and bylaws shape how these environments are built and maintained, influencing living conditions for both people and rats. Thinking about rats through municipal elections can offer a more tangible way to understand how complex it is to manage rats without addressing broader issues.

item.title: ‘Switzy’: In her new novel Emma Cline inhabits a man with dementia
item.description: ‘Switzy’ raises a difficult question: if life remains meaningful even in the face of decline, what exactly justifies bringing it to an end?
item.content:encoded:
Emma Cline is best known as the author of novels about troubled young women. The Girls, her debut, inhabited a follower of a Charles Manson figure, who opted out of the murders at the last minute. Her second, The Guest, followed a callow beauty who’d attached herself to a wealthy man for accommodation.

Switzy, her third novel, longlisted for this year’s Booker Prize, turns to a different kind of protagonist. The novel follows an elderly American man making a final journey to Switzerland. Rather than scrutinising the ethics of such a decision, Cline focuses on the stories we tell ourselves about ourselves, how we construct our own version of events, and what happens when our ability to control that narrative begins to slip away.

David is not an immediately sympathetic guide. He is often curt, entitled and rude, particularly towards his assistant, Cody (who is not altogether warm). item.title: In Colombo, toilets are missing from urban development plans, putting women’s health at risk
item.description: Sri Lanka’s capital has a severe paucity of crucial public hygiene facilities, with women bearing the brunt of this neglect.
item.content:encoded:
“Menstruating monthly is not an illness,” says Sumithra Randenigala, who works as a security guard in Sri Lanka’s largest city, Colombo. But when she has her monthly period, the 26-year-old often calls in sick to work.

Getting her pay docked some days each month is a better alternative than being unable to use the toilet during the two-hour daily train commute from her sleepy seaside town Bentota to Colombo Fort Station.

“If I need to change my pad, the toilet on the train is locked or blocked. At work, guards aren’t allowed to use the office toilet,” she tells me at the Sri Lanka Tea Board, where she works.

She attended school till age 14, where she learnt about urinary tract infections in class. She knows the importance of changing her sanitary pad frequently. After several painful experiences of contracting UTIs, she now chooses to forfeit her daily pay sometimes, rather than risk an infection that would force her to take a week of unpaid sick leave.

“And so they went on, throwing out truths without eye contact, the words so powerful neither of them could bear to behold their effect.”

In Louise Kennedy’s new novel, Stations, the Troubles in Northern Ireland are finally over.

item.title: How the British looted Indian property after the uprising of 1857 – and justified it
item.description: In diaries and written accounts, English officers and wives cheer on the plunder of Indian belongings as retribution and revenge for violence by sepoys.
item.content:encoded:
Crockery from the Awadh palace. Silver items and animals from Nana Saheb Peshwa’s Bithur palace. Ornaments and silk garments belonging to Mughal Emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar. These were among the items looted by the British during the uprising of 1857.

But looting, it seems from books written by British men and women who experienced the rebellion, was only what violent Indians did. Their accounts present a rather different framing of the marauding. Their descriptions of the plunder by the British suggest that they were heroes who were merely rectifying an unfortunate mistake.

Even as they expressed a fear of their belongings falling into Indian hands, British writers also describe indulging in the plunder and destruction of Indian property and cheering it on – despite a proclamation from the East India Company authorities forbidding this.

They did so with impunity, fearing neither social ostracisation nor judicial repercussions.

‘All we valued was lost to us…’

When the uprising began in Meerut on May 10, 1857, the looting was incidental since the focus of the sepoys of the East India Company was to punish their British officers.

But Delhi, where the sepoys went next, witnessed large-scale looting.

item.title: Flashback: When CEC Lyngdoh refused BJP demand for early Gujarat poll until voter roll was updated
item.description: The Election Commission insisted on remedying the list since many voters, especially Muslims, had been displaced from their homes after the 2002 riots.
item.content:encoded:
The deletion of nearly 13 crore names from the draft list as a result of the Special Intensive Revisions of electoral rolls under Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar has echoes of a controversy in Gujarat in 2002. The situation was similar, but the outcomes were different.

It was July 2002. Five months of sustained violence in the aftermath of the Godhra train burning in February that year had torn Gujarat apart. The post-Godhra attacks, largely on Muslims, had displaced thousands. Many had migrated from their homes and were living in relief camps.

In the middle of the mayhem, at 3 pm on July 19, Bharatiya Janata Party general secretary Arun Jaitley met with Chief Election Commissioner JM Lyngdoh. The situation in Gujarat is “normal”, Jaitley said, so why not hold early elections? If elections in Punjab and Assam could be held before normalcy had returned there, why not in Gujarat, he argued.

item.title: As Brazil votes again, Lula remains a crucial bulwark against Trump in the region

On October 25, Brazilians will return to the polls for the second round of the presidential election. The results will matter not only for the future of country itself, but also for the region and the world.

Alongside Canada and Mexico, Brazil, under the leadership of current President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, is one of the few countries in the region that has stood up to Donald Trump’s meddling and interference attempts.

The rise of the far right

Under Lula, Brazil still serves as a bulwark against the imposition of right-wing populist agendas critics say run counter to the broader interests of local societies, but cater to the interests of certain domestic elites. It is within this context that we must consider the Brazilian election alongside other electoral processes in the democratic world.

Many Trump-style leaders have recently come to power in the continent. The Economist compiled descriptive statistics to try to capture the trend. According to the publication, in 2023 there were two or three presidents aligned with Trump in the region. Today there are 11. If elected, Flávio Bolsonaro – son of jailed former president Jair Bolsonaro – would be the 12th. item.title: ‘Partita’: Barbara Kingsolver’s novel is about a musician bringing the rhythms of her life together
item.description: The novel is also a fascinating character study of women’s lives and relationships, and of changing American generations and traditions.
item.content:encoded:
A partita is a musical composition, often for a soloist. As Livia, the protagonist of Barbara Kingsolver’s new novel, Partita, explains to Sigurd, as they begin an all-consuming romance, it’s “made up of a lot of parts with different paces and moods. […] The parts are all different, and the artist’s work is to make them all add up to something that feels whole.”

Livia is just 20 at Indiana University, far from home, on a prestigious music scholarship. Distracted by the pursuit of excellence and the perfect love, she does not yet know that her life will be a partita, one she must make whole.

The contrasting parts of Livia’s life include three romantic relationships, an extraordinary piano talent, two bodily traumas, a fraught relationship with a violent, unloving mother, several losses, unspoken truths, loyal friends, and her brother’s suicide. The grief of losing her brother stifles Livia for decades. She focuses on piano virtuosity that takes her ever further from understanding herself – that is, until she is forced home.

item.title: In Goa, developers are grabbing eco-sensitive hilly land – ‘legally’
item.description: The state’s laws and curbs aimed at protecting the hills to prevent landslides are being systematically dismantled.

Right before the Mapusa river meets the Mandovi river near Panjim, it crosses the wetlands, creeks and low lying paddy fields of Salvador Do Mundo. Surrounding these large stretches of paddy fields are houses and forested hills with steep slopes. Telangana-based real-estate company, KGL Realtors Private Limited bought 20,000 square metres of land on one of these hills.

When the land was bought, the sale deed described it as “barren and waste land”. In Goa, a state-wide regional plan dictates what activities are permitted on a piece of land. The land that KGL bought is zoned as eco-sensitive land where development is regulated. It specifically categorises all of it as Natural Cover and part (4,000 square metres) of it as Natural Cover with “No Development Slopes”.

The Regional Plan 2021, published in 2010, marked nearly 82% of the state as eco-sensitive zones, providing them with protection from rampant construction and development.

item.title: Why the small town of Almora has instituted a literature festival
item.description: This year, the Almora Literature Festival will be held from October 30 to November 1. The inaugural edition took place in 2023.
item.content:encoded:
As Wikipedia notes, Almora is a municipal town and cantonment in Uttarakhand’s Kumaun region. It did not emerge from the pressures of recent urbanisation. Rather, it is a 600-year-old town situated on the Kashyap Hills. It sits on a 5-km-long mountain ridge that forms a distinct horseshoe shape.

Indeed, Almora is older than Kolkata, Chennai or Mumbai.

During the late 16th century, the Chanda rulers of Kali Kumaon (today’s Champawat) shifted their capital to Almora, which, in certain accounts, was referred to as Alamnagar. This is how the town is believed to have been founded. It later passed into the hands of the Gorkhas for a brief period and became part of British India in 1816, following the formalisation of the Treaty of Sugauli between the British and the Gorkhas.

Beyond this ruler-oriented history, Almora has a rich past of its own. Hailed as the cultural capital of Kumaun, it encompasses linguistic, literary, and spiritual history that give it the life of a thriving town.

Today, people often mistake Almora for another hill station with a Mall Road, bustling bazaars, cosy eateries, cosy cafés, colonial buildings and historical relics. Well, it has a bit of everything mentioned. Almora probably does not offer the instant tourist gratification of Nainital,...

A Delhi court on Friday extended till February the permission for United States citizen Matthew VanDyke and six Ukrainians to stay abroad while the investigation in an arms training case was pending, the Hindustan Times reported.

They had been arrested by the National Investigation Agency in March for allegedly having links to ethnic armed groups in Myanmar that are hostile to India.

The court allowed the seven foreign citizens to stay outside India after the agency said that it needed more time to investigate the case, the newspaper reported.

On September 24, VanDyke and the Ukrainians were allowed by the court to travel to their home countries for a month on the condition that they would return and cooperate with the investigation.

They had been directed to return to India after one month and inform the court of their return within 72 hours.

While VanDyke returned to India for the court hearing on Friday, the six Ukrainians did not.

The Ukrainians appeared through video conferencing, citing health problems, The New Indian Express reported. After their counsel submitted that they were unwell, the court extended the permission for them to stay outside India.

item.title: As memories become entangled with machines, who controls what we remember?
item.description: History could now be determined by algorithms.
item.content:encoded:
My phone chimed with an automated “memory” slideshow from an old trip, set to gentle music, the skies impossibly blue, the faces so bright. I watched it twice before realising what bothered me: I hadn’t chosen the photos, the order, or the mood. Something else had decreed what my holiday felt like. If the machine had the sky wrong, would I know? Is a memory still mine once something else has contrived it?

But how reliable are our memories anyway? Elizabeth Loftus, a pioneer in false memory research, proved decades ago that a single leading question can rewrite our recollections. Today, experts know that memory is actively rebuilt every time we remember.

The act of offloading memory onto external tools – like a simple notebook – blurs the line between the mind and the environment. This phenomenon, described as the “extended mind” by philosophers Andy Clark and David Chalmers, finds a modern parallel in media theory through the concepts of mediatisation and mediation, where historical reality is consumed in a pre-edited format.

item.title: ‘I write to instil self-confidence and a new consciousness in the Adivasi’: poet Jacinta Kerketta
item.description: ‘Having a relationship with the community enables honest writing, whether I am offering a critique or documenting situations.’
item.content:encoded:
Adivasi communities have been spoken of using the language of policy, anthropology and development, often by those who do not share their realities. Now, however, young Adivasi writers are reclaiming the right to narrate their own histories, philosophies and futures. Among the most influential voices in this movement is Jacinta Kerketta, whose poetry, journalism and essays bear witness to the intimate relationship between memory, land, language and resistance. Her work challenges dominant narratives while affirming Adivasi ways of knowing as living and evolving traditions.

In a conversation with Scroll, Kerketta reflected on memory as an indigenous archive, the ethics of writing from within the community, the politics of language and translation, women’s role in sustaining collective memory, and more. Excerpts from the interview:

Across your poetry collections, from Angor to Jadon Ki Zameen and Ishwar Aur Bazaar to Prem Mein Ped Hona, memory often appears not as an individual possession but as something held collectively by land, rivers, forests and communities.
